title: Corky Blisters, Bumps & Edema-Like Lesions
summary: Raised blisters or corky bumps can result from edema or intumescence, but similar surface changes may also come from pests, chemical injury, residue, or disease. Texture and environmental history are important discriminators.
patternQuestions: Are bumps concentrated on lower leaf surfaces, petioles, or stems?
Do fresh lesions begin as translucent or raised blisters and later become corky?
Were nights or low-light periods unusually humid with a wet root zone?
Are mites, insects, fungal structures, or residue visible under magnification?
discriminatingChecks: Inspect both leaf surfaces with magnification
Review irrigation timing, RH, airflow, and nighttime conditions
Track whether new lesions stop forming after moisture and transpiration balance improves
Compare multiple plants and cultivars for susceptibility
redFlags: Moving pests or eggs present
Lesions rapidly expanding or crossing into stems
Sporulation or soft tissue decay
Whole-crop progression independent of environmental changes
visualNeeds: Fresh blister versus corky lesion timeline

title: Bronzing, Stippling & Surface Scarring
summary: Fine pale dots, bronzing, silvering, or surface scars often trigger a pest suspicion, but spray injury, abrasion, and environmental damage can create similar patterns. Direct evidence of the causal organism matters.
patternQuestions: Are individual pale feeding points visible or is the tissue uniformly bronzed?
Are symptoms stronger on leaf undersides, along veins, or in exposed canopy zones?
Are webbing, fecal specks, cast skins, eggs, or mobile arthropods present?
Did the pattern appear after a spray, handling event, or environmental shift?
discriminatingChecks: Inspect leaf undersides and symptom edges with adequate magnification
Compare pest signs with the damage rather than diagnosing from scars alone
Review spray and handling history
Map injury against canopy exposure and airflow
redFlags: Rapid population increase of confirmed pests
Webbing or abundant eggs
Severe distortion of new growth
Damage spreading among plants without a shared spray or handling event
visualNeeds: Mite stippling versus thrips silvering plate

title: Leaf Cupping, Strapping & Epinasty
summary: Severely twisted, narrowed, cupped, or downward-bent new growth can arise from herbicide exposure, microscopic mites, root-zone or micronutrient stress, systemic pathogens, or other developmental injury. Distribution and exposure history are critical.
patternQuestions: Is the newest growth disproportionately affected?
Do multiple plant species show a similar pattern in the same location?
Is there a spatial gradient toward an intake, edge, doorway, or treated area?
Are microscopic mites or eggs present on growing tips?
discriminatingChecks: Map the symptom across the room, field, and nearby non-crop plants
Inspect growing tips with high magnification
Review nearby herbicide use and sprayer or ventilation history
Measure root-zone pH and EC
Use pathogen testing when propagation-linked systemic disease remains plausible
redFlags: Multiple species injured along the same exposure gradient
Microscopic pest confirmed
Shoot-tip death
Symptoms recurring through a propagation chain

title: Sudden Post-Spray Speckling & Scorch
summary: Spotting, bleaching, or scorch that appears after a foliar application should be investigated as a possible exposure event before being labeled disease or deficiency. Droplet pattern and timing are especially useful clues.
patternQuestions: Did symptoms begin within a plausible interval after a spray or chemical application?
Does injury match droplet coverage, treated zones, or exposed leaf surfaces?
Were lights, temperature, or humidity unusually intense around application time?
Did untreated plants or shielded leaves remain normal?
discriminatingChecks: Reconstruct the spray record and tank history
Compare treated and untreated tissue
Inspect lesions with magnification for pests or fungal structures
Track whether spots remain static after the event or continue expanding
redFlags: Continuing lesion expansion after the exposure has ended
Sporulation or soft decay
Confirmed pest population
Repeated injury from the same tank or application process

title: Patchy Container-to-Container Decline
summary: When neighboring plants decline unevenly, distribution can reveal irrigation, drainage, emitter, root disease, pest, media, or placement differences that would be hidden by looking only at one symptomatic plant.
patternQuestions: Do affected plants share an irrigation line, bench position, media batch, or runoff path?
Are containers drying at different rates?
Is the pattern clustered, random, edge-biased, or associated with one cultivar or propagation lot?
Are root symptoms similar across affected plants?
possibleCategories: Root disease spread through shared water
discriminatingChecks: Measure emitter output and container moisture across the pattern
Inspect roots from affected and unaffected plants
Map the problem against irrigation zones, airflow, temperature, and runoff
Review propagation and media lot records
redFlags: Rapid spread along shared water routes
Severe root sloughing
Blocked or failed emitters
Clusters linked to one propagation lot

title: Wet-Media Wilt & Post-Irrigation Droop
summary: A drooping plant in wet media may have impaired root aeration or root disease rather than a water shortage. The timing of wilt relative to irrigation can completely change the differential.
patternQuestions: Does droop begin or worsen after irrigation?
How long does the medium remain wet?
Are roots firm and actively branching or dark, soft, and reduced?
Does the plant improve as the root zone dries?
possibleCategories: Less likely true drought when the root zone is demonstrably wet
discriminatingChecks: Measure moisture and dryback rather than watering again by reflex
Inspect roots and drainage
Measure root-zone EC and temperature
Compare plants in faster- and slower-drying positions
redFlags: Root sloughing or strong decay odor
Rapid collapse across a shared irrigation system
Persistent saturation
No recovery as aeration improves
